newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: El Nino may boost Indonesian corn buying - trade.
newsitem.headline: El Nino may boost Indonesian corn buying - trade.

text.p: Indonesia may have to buy more than 200,000 tonnes of corn by the end of the year if a drought said to be linked to the El Nino weather anomaly savages the corn crop on Java, regional traders said on Thursday.
"Their corn imports could reach more than 200,000 tonnes, but the El Nino is the wild card in all this," a dealer for a commodity trading house in Singapore told Reuters.
"People are waiting to see how much damage the drought does to the crop on Java," another senior trader said.
Indonesian traders say the drought is seasonal and has nothing to do with El Nino.

El Nino, Spanish for Christ Child because it was first noticed by Peruvian anchovy fishermen around Christmas, can wreak havoc on weather-sensitive farming countries around the Asia-Pacific rim and beyond.
It forms when waters in the Pacific Ocean off Peru and Ecuador turn warmer, disrupting wind and other global weather patterns.
Scientists say the El Nino this year may rival the one in 1983, the largest this century, which caused billions of dollars in damage through drought, hurricanes and floods in more than 15 nations.
The 1983 El Nino caused withering drought in Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines and South Africa. Floods inundated India and Peru while severe winter storms lashed California.
Meteorologists meeting in Australia early this month said the current El Nino appears to have arrived early and could last longer than previous ones.
Indonesia has concluded deals in the last two weeks for 100,000 tonnes of corn for August arrival.
But the grains and oilseeds business in Thailand and Malaysia remained quiet.

Dealers said buyers were sitting back to watch if two rain systems expected to pass through the U.S. Midwest over the weekend will soak parched areas like Illinois and help drive down corn futures prices on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT).
"Everybody's on the sidelines for the next four to five days. Corn is pollinating and there is a big rain event from Saturday through Tuesday," one dealer said.
"If the rain comes in as expected, I presume we'll continue to go south on prices," the dealer added. "Nobody wants to do anything now. It's going to be a very nervous weekend."
Pollinations is the vital reproductive stage of development. Hot and dry weather hinders the formation of corn kernels and slices corn yields.
Dry weather has been forecast in key U.S.-corn growing states and the two rain systems are expected to help slake the thirst of corn plants.

"It's pretty simple. If the weather stays dry through next week, prices will climb. If we get rain, you'll see prices head the other way. Until then, the buyers will sit on the sidelines watching the weather like everyone else," a trader said.
Traders said sharp price fluctuations on the CBOT also discouraged buyers and kept them out of the market.
"One day it goes up and then it dives the following day. I think there's too much fluctuation for anybody to do business in this market," a dealer said.
The trade is also waiting for Thailand's final approval of a plan for the duty-free importation of 150,000 tonnes of corn.
"The decision should come in soon, but the Thais will probably just buy cargoes in transit like they did the last time," a dealer said.
- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
